paceDoctrine.headline: Daily floor protects the identity. Weekly total protects the progress.

rules.v: Touch the work. 20 minutes minimum, every day.
rules.why: This is the streak. It is about being someone who does this daily, not about volume.

rules.v: Hit the weekly hour target across six working days.
rules.why: This is the actual progress metric. A busy Tuesday is not a moral failure if the week lands.

rules.v: One deliberate rest day. Anki and the weekly review only.
rules.why: A rest day bridges the streak instead of breaking it. Fifty-two weeks without one is not a plan, it is a countdown.

rules.v: Sleep is a tracked input, not a residual.
rules.why: Spaced repetition works through sleep-dependent consolidation. Anki on six hours of sleep is theatre.

paceDoctrine.replaces: Replaces the “3 hours a day, not 2 hours 50 minutes” framing. Same weekly volume, survivable for a year.

habitStack.label: Anki spaced repetition
habitStack.detail: Reviews only. 10–15 min. The one habit that survives a rest day.

habitStack.label: DSA practice

habitStack.label: Deep implementation work

habitStack.label: Commit to GitHub, update project log
habitStack.detail: Never go a day without a commit.

habitStack.label: Lectures, code review, blog posts

habitStack.label: Write the daily log

habitStack.label: Lights out

scheduleModes.label: Normal
scheduleModes.note: 21 hours across six working days, roughly 3.5 h each. On good days you will overshoot.

scheduleModes.label: Semester
scheduleModes.note: Coursework is running. Your university maths modules ARE Phase 1 — do the overlap once, using lectures and roadmap practice together, and count those hours here.

scheduleModes.label: Exam week
scheduleModes.note: Target drops to 7 hours. DSA rises to 45 min to match coursework. Touch it daily and the streak holds.

scheduleModes.label: Break
scheduleModes.note: University holiday. This is when phases actually get finished. Still take the rest day — especially now.

stuckProtocol.hardStop: Never sit stuck for more than 1 hour without escalating to step 3 or beyond.

steps.label: Restate
steps.detail: Write the problem down in one sentence.

steps.label: Search
steps.detail: Google / StackOverflow for the exact error or concept.

steps.label: Ask AI
steps.detail: Paste code + error into Claude or ChatGPT. Ask for the explanation, never the fix.

steps.label: Community
steps.detail: Post in Discord with what you tried and what happened.

steps.label: Skip & return
steps.detail: Move to the next topic. Revisit tomorrow with fresh eyes.

aiAssistantRule.verdict: No Copilot, no Cursor, no autocomplete agent until Phase 1 is cleared.
aiAssistantRule.reasoning: The capability you need for interpretability research is holding a computation in your head and knowing what every tensor dimension means. That is built only by manual struggle. Let AI write your Phase 0 and Phase 1 code and you will ship working code while learning almost nothing.
allowed: Asking for an explanation of an error, a concept, or someone else's code
Asking why your approach is wrong after you have written it
Asking for a reading recommendation or a counter-argument
forbidden: Generating code you then paste and run
Autocomplete that finishes your line before you have thought it
Asking for the fix instead of the reason (Stuck Protocol step 3 says explanation, not fix)
aiAssistantRule.after: Once Phase 1's gate is cleared, assistants become a genuine multiplier. The rule has an expiry date, not a moral basis.

ankiDiscipline.headline: Three new cards a day. Self-made. Generative, not recognitive.

rules.k: Cap new cards at 3 per day
rules.v: Reviews compound at roughly 10x the new-card rate. Three a day is about 20 reviews a day at steady state — sustainable forever. Ten a day buries you by week five.
Skip the pre-made “ML Mathematics” decks. Writing the card is most of the learning; an imported deck gives you the reviews without the encoding.
A card should make you produce something, not recognise something.
If reviews exceed 25 minutes, you are over-creating. Suspend cards rather than skipping days.

examples.good: Write KL(P‖Q) and state which distribution the expectation is taken over.
Write the sliding-window template from memory and name two problems it solves.
Given A = UΣVᵀ, say what the columns of U mean geometrically.

writingRitual.headline: One short public explainer every week, starting in Phase 1.
writingRitual.spec: Explain the hardest thing you touched this week, in your own words, to someone one step behind you. 300–800 words. Post it publicly — a blog, a gist, a Discord thread, LessWrong shortform. Forty minutes.
why: Research is writing. You are practising the actual job from week four, not week thirty-one.
Writing exposes fake understanding within a paragraph. Nothing else does it as fast.
It builds the public trail that gets you into MATS. A trail of 40 explainers beats any CV.
writingRitual.seeds: Your daily log already captures “what confused me” and the weekly review captures your biggest insight. Those are the drafts. The ritual is making one of them public.

weeklyRituals.label: Weekly review answered honestly
weeklyRituals.detail: The seven questions. Ten minutes the first time, five after.

weeklyRituals.label: Public explainer published
weeklyRituals.detail: 300–800 words on the hardest thing this week.

weeklyRituals.label: Rest day taken
weeklyRituals.detail: Anki and the review only. No guilt, no catching up.

weeklyRituals.label: Anki audited
weeklyRituals.detail: Reviews under 25 min? If not, suspend cards — do not skip days.

weeklyRituals.label: Read someone else's code
weeklyRituals.detail: One real file from PyTorch, TransformerLens or a repo you use. Navigating unfamiliar code is a trained skill.

sustainability.headline: The plan has to survive contact with a first year of university.

points.v: A 06:00 start needs lights out by 22:30. If you were up late, skip the morning block — do not skip the sleep.
Weekly. Non-negotiable in the same way the work is.

points.k: No zero days, no hero days
points.v: A 12-hour Sunday to make up for a lost week is a fade in disguise. Log it, move on.
Switch to Exam mode rather than breaking the streak. The target moves; the habit does not.
Sick days are rest days. Streak bridges them the same way.

streakRecovery.action: No big deal. Tomorrow is Day 1 of a new streak. Zero guilt.
Minimum 20-minute session to restart. Open the editor and code anything.
Do the Weekly Review anyway. Identify what caused the break. Restart where you stopped.
Never go back to the beginning. Always resume from your current point.

passes.goal: Full read. Mark unknown equations. Summarize each section.
Re-derive key equations. Reimplement in code.

fieldDrift.headline: Hold the techniques loosely. Hold the fundamentals tightly.
fieldDrift.body: Sparse autoencoders were the interpretability frontier in 2023–24 and their limits are already under active debate. Whatever is hot when you reach Phase 3 may not be what you read about here. That is not a reason to change the plan — transformers, optimisation, probability and interpretability as a way of thinking do not rot. It is a reason to re-check the open-problems list when you arrive rather than treating it as canon.
durable: Reading a paper and reimplementing it
perishable: Which SAE architecture is state of the art
Whichever library wrapped the above this year

metaRules: Touch the work every day. 20 minutes counts. The weekly total is where volume lives.
Implement before you “understand.” Build first, understand through building.
Confusion is the signal, not the obstacle. Spend time on what confuses you.
Write your own code until Phase 1 is cleared. Ask AI for explanations, never for fixes.
Read source code. PyTorch internals. TransformerLens. Hugging Face.
Find your cohort. 2–5 people at your intensity level.
Publish one explainer a week. If you can't explain it, you don't know it.
Don't optimize prematurely. Momentum beats perfection.
Use the Stuck Protocol. Never spin for more than 1 hour.
Three new Anki cards a day, made by you. Reviews every morning.
Sleep is part of the curriculum. Protect the floor.
Streaks recover, and a rest day bridges them. Missing a day doesn't erase progress.

successMarkers.evidence: Dangerous in Python. Git fluent. First repo pushed. Can debug your own code.
Derive gradient descent on paper. A network you wrote from scratch learns something. 8+ public explainers.
A Transformer you built from a blank file generates text. Reading a paper a week.
Reimplement a Transformer from memory. Fine-tuned an LLM. 10+ papers, 8+ repos, blog running.
Working through ARENA. One mech interp result replicated. Known in two communities.
Original technical work published. Applied to MATS. A research agenda you can defend.

closingWarning: The biggest risk is not that this is too hard. It's that you'll start strong and fade. The antidote is your daily log, your Anki streak, your weekly explainer, and your cohort. When motivation dies — and it will — discipline and systems carry you through.

dsa.purpose: Build algorithmic thinking. Pass university DSA courses. Have enough CS fundamentals to write efficient ML code and handle technical interviews when the time comes.
dsa.philosophy: DSA is a supplement to your AI path, not the main event. 30–45 min a day is enough. Consistency over grinding.
dsa.warning: The DSA trap: many students spend 6–12 months doing nothing but LeetCode, believing it's the only path. For an AI safety career, DSA is a tool — not the destination. Your Transformer implementations and mech interp research are what set you apart, not your LeetCode count.

Add to Anki after every new pattern: when to use it, plus template code.

years.focus: Independent research / thesis in AI Safety

plays.text: Find a research advisor in Year 1, semester 2
plays.detail: AMENDMENT — the original said Year 2. Move it earlier, and change the approach. “Can I do research with you” gets ignored. “I reproduced Figure 3 of your 2024 paper, here is my repo, here is where my numbers diverged, do you have fifteen minutes” gets answered. You will be able to send that email once Phase 1 is cleared.

plays.text: Ask about GPU cluster access in semester one
plays.detail: AMENDMENT — the original filed this under Year 2. Ask now. The answer is often just “email this person”, and it is the queue, not the permission, that costs you time later.

plays.text: Start a reading group — 3–5 students, one safety paper a week
plays.detail: Running the group is worth several times more than attending one. Leading a discussion forces a depth of understanding that reading alone never produces.

plays.text: Do visible, useful work inside a community you joined
plays.detail: AMENDMENT — the original plan is passive: join, lurk, ask when stuck. That is consumption. Reproduce a result someone asked about. Write up a paper for the reading group. Answer the beginner questions you were asking three months ago. Being known is how you get into MATS, far more reliably than a CV.

plays.text: Apply to summer programs — SPAR first, then MATS
plays.detail: SPAR around the end of Phase 2, MATS once Phase 3 is underway. Sign up for MATS notifications now: applications open long before you will feel ready, and feeling ready is not the bar.

plays.text: Attend NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR virtually — free
plays.detail: Virtual attendance costs nothing, and the workshop tracks are where most of the safety work surfaces.
